title: Why Do Dogs Sniff Each Other's Butts? (The Real Reason)

script: Your dog just walked up to a total stranger and shoved its nose somewhere very rude. In dog language, that's actually one of the most polite things they can do. Underneath a dog's tail sit two small glands that produce a scent completely unique to that individual dog, packed with information: age, sex, health status, diet, even mood. To a dog's nose, one sniff reads almost like a full profile card, no words needed. This is also why the greeting is normally mutual, both dogs take turns, and that back and forth is itself part of the etiquette, a kind of trust exchange. When a dog refuses to let another sniff, or spins away and blocks access, that's often a sign of discomfort or distrust, the equivalent of pulling your hand away from a handshake. Compare that to a human handshake, which honestly tells you almost nothing, and a dog's version is doing far more real communication in just a few seconds. So next time it looks awkward at the park, remember, that's not weird behavior, that's your dog reading a business card the only way they know how. Understanding these small moments is a big part of understanding your dog's whole social world.
